22nd of April 2017

Why is now not a good time to pursue theoretical physics?

Before I begin, I would like to clarify a few things about what I am going to say.

First, I do not know very much about theoretical physics. I am only in the third year of my degree—I have not even been studying physics for three years—so I am probably wrong about many things, and I may think differently in the future. Nevertheless, I think my perspective could be interesting, especially to people who, like me, are thinking about their future in physics. My words should therefore be treated with caution, bearing in mind that they are highly speculative.

Second, I should clarify what I mean by theoretical physics. When I talk about theoretical physics, I am mainly referring to the following fields: cosmology, string theory and other attempts at unified theories, and particle physics. In other words, the most abstract and fundamental branches of physics. I am not including other fields, such as theoretical condensed matter physics.

In general, a person can have two reasons for pursuing science. The first is the desire to contribute to humanity’s scientific and technological progress and, broadly speaking, to improve people’s lives. The second is simply to satisfy their curiosity through what Richard Feynman called the pleasure of finding things out. In my opinion, a scientist should have both motivations. The first is more pragmatic and productive, but it does not always lead down pleasant paths. The second is more childish and selfish; nevertheless, we all need something to keep us going and help us avoid losing our way along those devilish paths. We often achieve wonderful things by doing what we enjoy. I therefore believe that anyone who pursues science should strike a balance between these two motivations, without getting lost in absurd speculation simply for personal satisfaction, but also without becoming discouraged by a lack of satisfaction along the way.

I think we all agree that to be a theoretical physicist who makes a meaningful contribution to the field, you need to be extraordinarily intelligent. And, as an intelligent person, you should care about making the best use of your efforts. Anyone who has ventured even a little into research—not just theoretical physics, but any reasonably established branch of knowledge—will know that the amount of information out there is immeasurable. Until relatively recently, most people could not access higher education, which meant that the few individuals who managed to stand out in a field became well known and had the opportunity to make major advances. Mind you, this does not mean it was easy, or that those people were not brilliant: they were. However, we live at a time when there are more people on Earth than ever before, and a greater proportion of them have access to the education needed to pursue higher studies.

Never in human history have so many geniuses had access to education. Yet you could stop someone on the street and ask them to name a famous scientist born after 1950, and probably no one would be able to name one. The reason is not that these people are uneducated, but that there are virtually NO famous scientists born after 1950.

This is by no means a bad thing. There are currently more scientists than ever, and scientific and technological development is moving faster than at any previous point in history, so it is natural that individuals find it harder to stand out. However, this overwhelming scientific progress is making it increasingly difficult for any one person to reach the frontier of knowledge. By the frontier of knowledge, I mean the point in a field where no one yet knows how to proceed, and where researchers must stand at the spearhead of science to forge a path through the darkness of ignorance.

For example, someone who wants to pursue string theory needs an enormous amount of study and hard work before they can actually begin doing research in it. They must have a deep understanding of classical physics, analytical mechanics, quantum mechanics, particle physics, multilinear algebra and tensor analysis, the calculus of variations, topology, differential geometry, group theory, general relativity… In short, an endless list of things you are required to know before you can do anything even remotely worthwhile. A person has about 50 years of their life to devote to physics: from the age of 18, when the education system allows them to focus entirely on physics, until retirement. In the past, 50 years was enough time to reach the frontier of knowledge and start doing new things. But as science advances, that amount of time becomes increasingly inadequate, because there is more and more to learn. What is more, new papers by physicists around the world appear every day, and you have to read—and understand—them to stay up to date. In other words, more things are added to what you need to study while you are still studying, and at a faster rate than any one person can learn. This is the first problem facing a student who wants to pursue theoretical physics. If you want to contribute something—one of the motivations a scientist ought to have—you are pressed for time. We are approaching a point where a human lifetime will not be long enough to get to the stage of doing research.

The next question a student who wants to pursue theoretical physics should ask is: to what extent is it worth it? We have already said that to pursue theoretical physics, you have to be very smart and work very hard—and when I say very hard, I mean it. Is this really the best way for someone like that to use their time and intelligence? Let us return to string theory, perhaps the most illustrative example.

String theory is a speculative theory of fundamental physics that aims to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein’s theory of gravitation. It is a fascinating theory that has generated a great deal of fruitful research in fields ranging from pure mathematics to more mundane activities, such as simplifying routine calculations of cross sections in particle physics. However, its distinctive predictions could only be tested if we had accelerators capable of reaching the Planck mass scale—more than 16 orders of magnitude more powerful than the LHC in Geneva. This is not even conceivable today, nor is it in the foreseeable long-term future. The fact that it is practically impossible to test empirically—a scientific theory must be falsifiable—gives rise to profound debates between string theorists and physicists in other fields. In other words, the thing you are going to devote your entire life to will probably be nothing more than a fiendishly difficult puzzle that cannot be empirically verified and may well be false. Will it be worth it? That depends entirely on which of the two motivations I mentioned earlier you take refuge in. From the pragmatic perspective, the most likely answer is no: it will not be worth it. From the perspective of the pleasure of finding things out, things may be different, since you have an enormous amount of information ahead of you to discover.

So, should human beings stop pursuing theoretical physics? In my view, yes—but with a catch. To explain my position, let us recall the following saying: “Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach him to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.” Something similar is going to happen in scientific research, with computers taking the place of fishing. Artificial intelligence will arrive sooner or later—probably sooner rather than later, and certainly before humanity obtains an accelerator that can confirm string theory. When it does, human beings will be unable to compete with a machine connected to the internet and possessing a capacity for processing and thought beyond human imagination. Perhaps the conclusions a theoretical physicist reaches through an entire lifetime of work will be reached by an artificial intelligence in just a few minutes. Doing research will become as absurd as spending an entire night performing calculations, as physicists once did, when those same calculations can now be done with a single line of MATLAB code.

For these reasons, I believe theoretical physics is one of the most misguided choices for someone with a remarkable intellect, at least from the standpoint of the pragmatic motivation for scientific activity.

What, then, should someone who wants to contribute to theoretical physics devote themselves to? To helping invent the computers that will carry out that research. Right now, there are many open lines of research in artificial intelligence, both in software—machine learning—and in hardware—quantum computing, neuroscience, and so on. Who makes better use of their time: the person who develops an excellent scientific theory, or the person who builds a machine capable of creating countless magnificent scientific theories?

Zimbabwe Can Leverage Google Expertise to Accelerate Its Digital Ambitions

President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s meeting with Google Senior Vice President James Manyika highlights an increasingly important opportunity for Zimbabwe: turning relationships with global technology leaders into practical capabilities that can support the country’s digital transformation.

Manyika, a Zimbabwean-born technology executive with a senior role at Google, brings extensive experience at the intersection of technology, artificial intelligence, data, economic development and the future of work. His expertise offers Zimbabwe a valuable connection to some of the forces reshaping economies around the world.

For Zimbabwe, the opportunity goes beyond the symbolism of a meeting between a national leader and a global technology executive. The more consequential question is how the country can translate such engagements into knowledge, investment, skills and technology that benefit citizens and businesses.

Zimbabwe has a young population and an expanding technology ecosystem.

Access to expertise from people operating at the highest levels of the global technology industry could help strengthen conversations around artificial intelligence, digital skills, entrepreneurship, cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure and the use of technology in public services.

The potential value is also strategic.

Countries that successfully participate in the digital economy will increasingly depend not only on physical infrastructure, but on human capital, technological know-how and connections to global innovation networks. Zimbabwe can seek to use relationships such as this to expose its entrepreneurs, universities, policymakers and technology professionals to international expertise and opportunities.

The meeting also reflects a broader diplomatic approach that President Mnangagwa has described through the phrase “friend to all, enemy to none.” Whatever one's assessment of that foreign-policy approach, engagement with influential global technology companies demonstrates how diplomatic relationships can potentially open channels beyond traditional politics and trade.

The opportunity now is to make such engagement tangible.

Google’s global expertise, combined with Zimbabwean talent and local knowledge, could potentially contribute to initiatives in areas such as AI education, digital entrepreneurship, technology-enabled public services and skills development. 

The greatest benefit would come if high-level engagements lead to sustained programmes rather than remaining isolated diplomatic encounters.

Manyika's Zimbabwean roots add another dimension to that possibility.

His understanding of the country's context, combined with his experience in global technology, creates a potentially useful bridge between Zimbabwean ambitions and the rapidly changing international technology landscape.

For Zimbabwe, the message is therefore bigger than one meeting. Global expertise is an asset, and the country has an opportunity to connect that expertise with its own talent, institutions and ambitions.

The challenge is to convert access into action: partnerships into programmes, expertise into skills, and conversations into measurable digital opportunities for Zimbabweans.

That is where engagements with leaders such as Manyika could become particularly consequential for Zimbabwe's digital future.

Osun election has shown how much the electorates want credible, free and fair elections. It also showed how demand side of electoral accountability combined human network and artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver real time information about the process, the incidence, and the results from the votes.

On the side of political actors, we continue to see how video, voice and visual contents are being generated using AI. There’s also the understanding that INEC will use the tool of AI to ensure effective delivery of a credible election come the general elections in 2027.

There are various opportunities for all sides of the table to use AI constructively or corrosively during the 2027 elections. Yet, the real question remains whether AI is the most important factor that will shape how the mandates of the people, INEC and political parties will be upheld. 

There is also the question whether the digital system that AI rests on in Nigeria is robust enough to protect rights and interests of all parties as we get close to the elections.

How well prepared are the media, civil society, courts, lawmakers and the international observers for the elections? How much hype is given to AI? How much intentionality is given to past trends in the use of technology in our elections?

These issues and the opportunity for technologists and other stakeholders to get their hands dirty to build tools and learn from each other are packed into this event come 14-15 October, 2026.

@Dataphytefdn is proud to be a partner alongside @YIAGA, @CJIDAfrica, @inecnigeria and others to bring you this exciting event.

Stay tuned.
